resources.string: The upper part of the brainstem surrounds the cerebral aqueduct and lies just above the pons.
This narrow channel passes through the midbrain and carries cerebrospinal fluid from the third ventricle to the fourth.
The middle part of the brainstem forms the rounded bulge at the front. Its back helps form the floor of the fourth ventricle.
This fluid-filled space lies between the cerebellum behind it and the pons and upper medulla in front of it.
The medulla lies below the pons and tapers into the spinal cord.
Cerebellum, midline section through the vermis (front at left)
In this midline view, the smaller anterior lobe lies above and in front of the primary fissure.
This deep groove separates the anterior and posterior lobes of the cerebellum.
The larger posterior lobe extends behind and below the primary fissure.
Branches of white matter extend from the center into the folds, forming a tree-like pattern in this section.
These narrow, leaf-like folds give the outer cerebellar cortex its ridged surface.
Spinal cord, transverse section (back at top)
This shallow groove marks the middle of the back of the spinal cord. The anterior median fissure on the opposite side is deeper.
The slender rear projection of gray matter receives and processes incoming sensory information.
This tiny channel lies in the bridge of gray matter connecting the two halves of the cord.
White matter surrounds the butterfly-shaped gray matter and contains bundles of nerve fibers that travel along the cord.
The broader front projection of gray matter contains motor neurons whose axons reach skeletal muscle.
This deep cleft runs along the midline at the front of the spinal cord.
